transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what finally got me to come in is… I’m having trouble following people when they’re talking right to me. Like at the museum—I'm there sometimes when they’re planning the next art walk, and I’ll be looking straight at the person, nodding along, and then suddenly I realize I missed the middle of what they said. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again.

It’s a little embarrassing, you know. And the art walks are nice, actually—last one had this local watercolor fellow, really good with skies—but anyway, that’s the kind of thing. I’m present, but I don’t seem to catch all of it.
Do you notice this problem more when there's background noise or when people speak softly or in a higher pitch, compared to quiet, one-on-one conversations?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed it that way exactly. I mean, if there’s a lot going on around me, sure, that can make it harder to keep track, but I can’t say I’ve paid attention to whether it’s because someone talks softly or has a higher voice.

Sometimes even when it’s just one person talking, I’ll catch myself drifting a bit. But the noise thing… I’d have to think about that. I was at this café last week—well, it wasn’t really a café, more like one of those places with the pastries in the glass case—and I remember the espresso machine was loud, but I don’t know if that’s the same sort of thing you mean.
Do you also notice your mind drifting or losing focus during other activities—like reading, watching TV, or doing tasks at work—not just when someone is talking to you?

Yes, reading especially. I’ll sit down with a gallery packet, or notes for one of the art walk things, and I start out all right. Then a few minutes in, my eyes are still going down the page, but I’m off thinking about something else completely.

Then I realize I didn’t take in any of it and I have to go back and read the same paragraph again. Sometimes more than once. It’s funny, the packets have all these little bios and schedules, and I’ll think, “Oh, this is simple enough,” and then suddenly I’m halfway down the page and couldn’t tell you what I just read.

Has this kind of trouble focusing and following conversations been something you've dealt with since childhood or young adulthood, or is this a new change that's developed more recently, like in the past several months or years?

No, it’s not really new. I mean, I’ve probably been this way a long time. Even back in grade school, I remember my report cards would say things like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.”

My mother used to sit beside me when I did homework, just to keep me on track. This was before I was twelve, I think. She’d be at the kitchen table with me—well, we had this little table near the window—and she’d keep bringing me back to the worksheet or whatever it was. So… yes, it goes way back.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a longstanding, pervasive pattern of inattentiveness—difficulty sustaining attention in conversations, losing track while reading, needing to reread material, and being easily distracted—that began before age 12 (documented via childhood report cards noting daydreaming and need for reminders, and parental supervision of homework).
